detail: Patch a square-wave output into a VCA and give it a simple envelope. Leave effects off until the basic voice feels useful.
Use a sine as the only audio source. Establish pitch, level, and phrasing before adding another waveform.
Build a simple triangle-wave voice with a VCA and envelope. Choose a register before adding modulation.
Patch a saw through a low-pass filter and VCA. Begin with modest resonance and shape the cutoff by hand.
Use a pulse-width control to choose a narrow but audible pulse. Hold its width steady while you establish a phrase.
Patch white noise through a filter and VCA. Use an envelope to make a clearly defined event.
Set a band-pass filter to a useful region, then shape the result with a VCA. Begin with one repeated sound.

prompt: Start with one oscillator and no filter.
detail: Patch the oscillator through a VCA and shape its amplitude. Choose the waveform directly rather than relying on a filter sweep.

prompt: Start with two oscillators in unison.
detail: Tune two oscillators to the same pitch and mix them at conservative levels. Begin without detuning or effects.

prompt: Start with a quiet FM tone.
detail: Use a suitable oscillator FM input with modulation depth near zero. Increase depth gently, then hold a setting while shaping the voice.

prompt: Start with a wavetable held still.
detail: Choose one wavetable position and leave scanning off. Establish an envelope and phrase before moving through the table.
Choose a sample and play it without layering. Set its level, playback range, and envelope before adding processing.
Use D, E, F, G, A, B, and C. Return to D as your home note; start with a short phrase before using the whole scale.
Use C, D, E, F, G, A, and B. Begin and resolve phrases on C before adding wider movement.
Use A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. Keep A as the tonal center while building a small repeating phrase.
Use E, F, G, A, B, C, and D. Make E the home note and try a phrase using E, F, and G first.
Use F, G, A, B, C, D, and E. Hold or return to F and include B in a short phrase.
Use G, A, B, C, D, E, and F. Treat G as home rather than simply running up the notes of C major.
Use D, E, F, G, A, Bb, and C. Build a short pattern that repeatedly returns to D.
Use E, F#, G, A, B, C, and D. Choose three or four of those notes for the first phrase.
Use G, A, B, C, D, E, and F#. Start with G as your reference and keep the first melody short.
Use C, D, Eb, F, G, Ab, and Bb. Begin with C, Eb, and G, then add other notes as needed.
Use F, G, A, Bb, C, D, and E. Establish F as home before extending the phrase.

prompt: Use only D, F, A, and C.
detail: Choose these four pitches in any octave. Build the first pattern without adding another pitch.
Use 80 BPM as the initial quarter-note pulse. Start with one event per beat before choosing a subdivision.
Use 120 BPM as the initial quarter-note pulse. Establish a simple pattern before adding clock divisions.
Start at 140 BPM with a sparse pattern. Leave enough empty steps to hear the spacing clearly.
Trigger one voice on each beat. Keep the pattern even while choosing pitch and articulation.
Divide each quarter-note beat into two events. Begin with an even pattern and a single voice.
Divide each beat into four steps. Activate only a few steps before filling out the pattern.
Set a sequence length of three and use a steady clock. Choose a small pitch set and let it repeat.
Use five steps at a consistent rate. Establish the loop without forcing it into a longer pattern yet.
Choose seven steps and a steady clock. Keep timbre fixed while you find the first phrase.

prompt: Start with one hit every two beats.
detail: Use a half-note event at your chosen tempo. Let the silence and decay occupy the space between hits.

prompt: Start with hits on steps 1, 4, and 7.
detail: Use an eight-step loop and activate only steps 1, 4, and 7. Keep the initial sounds identical.

prompt: Start with a rest on the first step.
detail: Use a short sequence with step 1 muted. Establish the other events before deciding whether the opening silence should remain.
Use a fast attack, short decay, and little or no sustain. Let each note fall away before the next one.
Set the attack near one second and use a gate long enough to hear the rise. Begin with a held or slowly changing pitch.
Use a release around two seconds as a starting point. Space the gates so you can hear how the notes overlap.
Hold a gate high and shape the sound while it remains open. Establish a steady tone before adding separate note events.
Set sustain to zero and use attack and decay to define each note. Begin with one repeated trigger.
Keep the voice open between connected notes, using your sequencer or envelope behavior as available. Begin with a slow two-note phrase.
Use short gates and an envelope that leaves audible gaps. Keep the pitches simple while defining the phrasing.

prompt: Start with a swell and a quick ending.
detail: Choose a slow attack and short release. Use gates long enough to reach the top of the swell.

prompt: Start with a sharp attack and a long tail.
detail: Use a quick attack and a longer decay or release. Leave space between events so the tail remains audible.
Build a voice whose filter opens briefly on each event. Keep the amplitude contour simple while choosing the filter movement.
Set a consistent gate length for every event. Establish the pattern before varying its articulation.

prompt: Start with alternating short and long gates.
detail: Use the same pitch for both gate lengths. Choose envelope settings that make the difference in duration easy to hear.
Leave delay and reverb out of the audio path. Establish the voice and phrasing before choosing an acoustic space.
Build a centered mono signal. Work on tone and arrangement before introducing stereo movement.
Choose a short room-like reverb at a low wet level. Keep the source clearly in front of its tail.

prompt: Start with a long reverb tail.
detail: Choose a long decay and play sparse events. Set wet level conservatively so the source is still identifiable.
Use a delay with low feedback so the first repeat is the main response. Set its level below the dry event.
Match the delay time to one quarter-note beat at your tempo. Begin with low feedback and a quiet return.
Set the delay to three quarters of a quarter-note beat. Use a sparse source pattern and low feedback first.
Try a short delay around 90 ms and low feedback. Keep the dry source louder than the repeat.

prompt: Start with a narrow stereo image.
detail: Keep both channels close to center. Introduce width only after the basic sound and phrase are established.

prompt: Start with a dry bass and a wet lead.
detail: Keep the lower voice direct and add a modest effect return to the higher voice. Begin with one simple part in each register.

prompt: Start with the effect return very quiet.
detail: Set a dry sound first, then raise the return just enough to notice. Use that as the initial balance.

prompt: Start with a long gap between sounds.
detail: Trigger one event, listen through its tail, and wait before the next. Set the pacing from what you can actually hear.
Set a conservative listening level and a clear, unclipped signal path. Build the patch without relying on loudness for excitement.
Choose soft, medium, and strong amplitudes. Apply them to an otherwise simple repeated event.

prompt: Start with an accent every fourth event.
detail: Keep pitch and timing steady. Raise the amplitude of every fourth event without clipping the output.

prompt: Start with every second note quieter.
detail: Alternate two amplitude levels. Keep gate length and timbre the same initially.
Use one phrase that moves from quiet to louder. Leave pitch and rhythm unchanged while setting the amplitude range.
Let a repeating phrase become progressively quieter. Keep the final events audible enough to hear their role.

prompt: Start with one quiet voice and one louder voice.
detail: Give the parts clearly different amplitude roles. Use simple material so their balance is the first decision.
Make every event the same level. Establish the pattern before deciding where emphasis belongs.
Hold pitch and timbre steady and use a slow control on a VCA. Begin with modest depth around an audible level.
Close the VCA, then open it with an envelope or manual gesture. Build the first phrase from deliberate entrances and exits.

prompt: Start with a soft ending to each phrase.
detail: Reduce the amplitude of the last event in a short loop. Keep the rest of the pattern even.

prompt: Start with one accent per phrase.
detail: Choose a single event to emphasize in each repeat. Leave the other events quieter and comparable in level.
Keep the clock even and swing off. Choose a simple rhythm before introducing any timing variation.
Apply a modest amount of swing to an eighth- or sixteenth-note pattern. Keep the sound consistent while choosing the feel.
Choose a steady tempo but place the main accents farther apart. Let the subdivisions stay available without filling every one.
In a four-beat bar, place a clear accent on beats 2 and 4. Begin with a minimal supporting pulse.
Use a steady beat as your reference and emphasize the events between beats. Keep the first pattern sparse.
Count three quarter-note beats per bar and emphasize beat 1. Build a short phrase inside that grouping.
Group five quarter-note beats as 3 plus 2. Make the first beat of each group audible before adding complexity.
Group seven quarter-note beats as 4 plus 3. Use accents to establish that grouping.

prompt: Start with a slow, even drone.
detail: Use a held sound and one slow modulation. Avoid rhythmic triggers until its movement has a clear pace.
Trigger a simple voice by hand rather than from a clock. Find a comfortable spacing and repeat it.

prompt: Start with a two-beat call and response.
detail: Use one short gesture for the first two beats and a related answer for the next two. Begin with the same sound for both.

prompt: Start with a repeating triplet figure.
detail: Fit three evenly spaced events into one quarter-note beat. Use only a few pitches while the subdivision becomes clear.
Tune one oscillator to a comfortable bass-register C. Shape a simple sound before introducing a sequence.
Choose a D that sits comfortably above the bass range. Keep it as the first reference while shaping the voice.

prompt: Start with a high, quiet tone.
detail: Choose an upper-register pitch and keep monitoring conservative. Use a simple envelope before adding another layer.
Keep the initial pitch sequence inside one octave. Make the first phrase with a small number of notes.

prompt: Start with two octaves of separation.
detail: Choose two voices with the same pitch class, two octaves apart. Balance them before adding independent melodies.

prompt: Start with a bass voice only.
detail: Build a lower-register voice and a short phrase. Leave the upper register empty until the bass has a clear role.
Keep the first voice in the middle or upper register. Build the initial texture without a low anchor.

prompt: Start with a rising four-note shape.
detail: Choose four pitches that move upward within a modest range. Repeat the contour before changing its direction.

prompt: Start with a falling four-note shape.
detail: Choose four pitches that move downward. Keep rhythm and articulation even while you establish the contour.
Repeat one note and vary nothing but its placement or duration. Add another pitch only after the phrase feels intentional.
Alternate a root and its octave. Keep the first rhythm simple enough to hear the register change.

prompt: Start with two voices in the same register.
detail: Choose nearby ranges and simple contrasting tones. Establish how the voices share that space before spreading them apart.
Use C and G, or transpose both notes together. Leave out the third while choosing texture and phrasing.
Use D and F as the first two pitches. Try them held together or alternating in a simple pattern.
Use C and E as your initial pitch pair. Hold or alternate them before adding another interval.

prompt: Start with a C major triad.
detail: Use C, E, and G. Play them together if available, or sequence them as a short arpeggio.

prompt: Start with a D minor triad.
detail: Use D, F, and A. Begin with a slow arpeggio or a sustained voicing.
Use C, F, and G. Keep E out of the initial phrase and listen to the resulting shape.

prompt: Start with a root and a ninth.
detail: Use C and the D above the next C. Let the wider interval define the first sound.
Use E and F at a comfortable register and low level. Hold them or alternate them deliberately.
Use C, D, E, F#, G#, and A#. Pick a few of these pitches for the first pattern.
Use A, C, D, E, and G. Keep the first phrase inside one octave.
Use C, D, E, G, and A. Establish a short repeating phrase before changing its note set.

prompt: Start with a root drone and two melody notes.
detail: Hold D as a drone and use F and A above it. Begin with slow changes so the relationships remain clear.

prompt: Start with a slow triangle LFO.
detail: Send a slow triangle to one suitable parameter through attenuation. Keep its range small while establishing the sound.

prompt: Start with a slow sine LFO.
detail: Use a smooth cycle lasting several seconds. Apply it gently to one destination and leave other modulation disconnected.
Sample a control source at a steady, slow rate. Attenuate the result before applying it to a suitable destination.

prompt: Start with a four-step filter pattern.
detail: Choose four cutoff levels and repeat them at a steady rate. Keep the oscillator pitch fixed initially.

prompt: Start with a filter sweep by hand.
detail: Build a simple voice and move cutoff manually. Choose a useful range before automating it.

prompt: Start with one envelope controlling two destinations.
detail: Send a contour to amplitude and one tone parameter, attenuating as needed. Establish useful ranges for both.
Use a pulse waveform and a slow modulation at low depth. Keep the width away from silent extremes.
If stereo panning is available, move one voice gently between channels. Keep the rest of the patch still.

prompt: Start with a held random value.
detail: Generate or choose one random control value and hold it for a whole phrase. Change it only at the next phrase boundary.

prompt: Start with every fourth gate opening a filter.
detail: Use a regular event stream and a slower accent contour on cutoff. Keep the filter movement small at first.

prompt: Start with an envelope you trigger by hand.
detail: Send a manual trigger to a contour and use it to shape one voice. Find a useful gesture before adding a clock.
Set the sound using fixed controls and a simple note pattern. Add movement only after the starting tone is clear.
